title: Agents & Harnesses
blurb: Agents and harnesses are a craft of their own. This stage is a deliberate SUMMARY — enough to fit them into the career path. For the depth dive, see the sideways peer at the bottom of this stage: harness-engineer-roadmap.

nodes.label: Tool use
nodes.description: What it means for an LLM to call a tool, how the model decides, how tool outputs come back. The basic building block of every agent.
nodes.doneWhen: You can build a single-tool agent and explain the control flow on a whiteboard.

resources.title: Building effective agents
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: The single most-cited practitioner essay on agents. The framing 'workflows vs agents' is now field-standard vocabulary.

resources.title: Anthropic — Tool use overview
resources.annotation: The canonical reference for the tool-use flow: schema, model call, tool result, continue. Read once.

resources.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
resources.author: Schick et al.
resources.annotation: The paper that established self-supervised tool use. Useful as context for where the field came from.

nodes.label: Function calling & MCP
nodes.description: Provider function-calling APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI) and Model Context Protocol — the emerging cross-provider standard for tool exposure.
nodes.doneWhen: You can wire a tool via function calling and via MCP and explain which to use when.

resources.title: Model Context Protocol
resources.annotation: The open standard for connecting tools and data to agents. Read the spec overview first, then the SDK quickstart.

resources.title: MCP Servers (reference implementations)
resources.annotation: Working MCP servers for filesystem, git, GitHub, browser, and more. The fastest path to understanding the protocol concretely.

nodes.label: Planning patterns
nodes.description: ReAct, chain-of-thought, plan-and-solve, tree-of-thought, reflexion. A taxonomy of how agents structure their reasoning loops.
nodes.doneWhen: You can name three planning patterns and explain when each is appropriate.

resources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
resources.author: Yao et al.
resources.annotation: The ReAct paper. The thought / action / observation loop became the default mental model for tool-using agents.

resources.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
resources.author: Shinn et al.
resources.annotation: Self-reflection as a planning improvement. The paper that established 'let the agent critique its own trace' as a pattern.

resources.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
resources.author: Yao et al.
resources.annotation: Search over thought trees. The right reference when sequential CoT isn't enough.

nodes.label: Memory & context engineering
nodes.description: Conversation memory, vector memory, scratchpads, context compaction, summarization. The agent equivalent of working memory and long-term memory.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe two memory patterns and the trade-offs between context-window pressure and recall.

resources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: The current best treatment of context-as-a-managed-resource: what to compact, what to surface, what to forget.

resources.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
resources.author: Packer et al.
resources.annotation: The OS-shaped memory hierarchy framing. The paper has aged well; the pattern shows up in most modern long-running agents.

nodes.label: Multi-agent coordination
nodes.description: Multi-agent debate, orchestrator-worker, role specialization, agent-to-agent protocols. When the extra complexity pays off and when it doesn't.
nodes.doneWhen: You can argue for or against multi-agent for a given task and not just default to it.

resources.title: Don't Build Multi-Agents
resources.author: Cognition
resources.annotation: The counter-argument every multi-agent enthusiast should read. Frames the context-passing problem clearly.

resources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: The case where multi-agent wins, written by a team that shipped it. Read it after the Cognition counter-argument.

nodes.label: Harnesses / scaffolds (the concept)
nodes.description: What a harness is — the surrounding code that turns an LLM into an autonomous agent. Read this node, then go sideways: harness-engineer-roadmap is the depth dive on this craft.
nodes.doneWhen: You can articulate what a harness is and what makes a harness good or bad.

resources.title: harness-engineer-roadmap
resources.annotation: The depth roadmap for this whole stage. Open it when you want to specialize in the harness craft.

resources.title: Building effective agents
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: Reread with the harness lens: what the scaffold does, what the model does, where the boundary should live.

nodes.label: Agent evaluation
nodes.description: End-to-end task evals (SWE-bench, WebArena, τ-bench), per-step evals, tool-call accuracy. Why agent eval is harder than LLM eval.
nodes.doneWhen: You can design an eval suite for an agent and explain why a single end-to-end score isn't enough.

resources.title: SWE-bench
resources.annotation: The standard end-to-end coding-agent benchmark. The leaderboard tells you the state of the field at a glance.

resources.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
resources.author: Yao et al.
resources.annotation: The right multi-turn tool-use benchmark. The user-simulator design is what makes the evaluation realistic.

resources.title: Inspect — AI safety evaluation framework
resources.annotation: UK AISI's framework. The most-extensible open agent-eval harness; tasks, scorers, and a structured tracing model.

nodes.label: Agent safety
nodes.description: Prompt injection in tool outputs, indirect injection from web content, action authorization, blast-radius limiting, observability. Agents have an attack surface that ordinary LLM apps do not.
nodes.doneWhen: You can list five concrete attack vectors against an agent and a mitigation for each.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
resources.annotation: The community-maintained taxonomy of LLM-app vulnerabilities. Read it once and the rest of agent-security writing makes sense.

resources.title: Prompt Injection — Simon Willison
resources.author: Simon Willison
resources.annotation: The single best running coverage of prompt injection in the wild — direct, indirect, exfiltration. Updated for years.

nodes.label: Computer-use agents
nodes.description: Agents that drive a real computer: screen capture, mouse, keyboard, no purpose-built APIs. Anthropic's Computer Use (Oct 2024) was the first frontier-lab implementation; OpenAI's Operator and others followed. The pattern raises the agent surface area dramatically — and the safety bar with it.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe how a computer-use agent grounds its actions in screen pixels and name two failure modes that browser-API or function-call agents do not have.

resources.title: Introducing computer use, a new Claude 3.5 Sonnet
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: The launch post. The clearest framing of what computer-use changes about agent architecture and why pixel-counting is the load-bearing detail.

resources.title: Computer use tool — Claude API documentation
resources.author: Anthropic
resources.annotation: The reference docs. Read for the actual tool schema and the prompt-engineering patterns the docs recommend — those are the load-bearing operational details.

resources.title: Initial explorations of Anthropic's new Computer Use capability
resources.author: Simon Willison
resources.annotation: The practitioner's first read. Captures the day-one excitement and the immediate prompt-injection-via-screen concern that every computer-use deploy needs to think about.

sidewaysLinks.label: Going deep on this stage → harness-engineer-roadmap
sidewaysLinks.blurb: This stage summarizes agents and harnesses as one stop on the AI-engineer career path. The peer roadmap goes the whole way: building harnesses end-to-end — scaffolds, control loops, sandboxing, eval, hardening. Open it when you're ready to specialize.
